title: Palindrome Number
directAnswer: If `n < 0`, return false. Otherwise reverse the digits and check equality with the original.

remember.takeaway: Save the original value before any loop mutates it.

problemStatement: Given an integer `n`, return whether it reads the same forwards and backwards. Negative numbers are never palindromes.
understanding: Reverse the number and compare with the original. Negatives fail immediately because of the leading minus sign.

approaches.name: Reverse and compare
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
A number is a palindrome when reversing its digits yields the same number. Reuse the reverse-a-number idiom and compare the reversed value to the original.

**Why save the original first.** The reversal loop destroys n (it divides it down to 0), so you must capture `original = n` *before* the loop, then compare `rev == original` afterward. Comparing against the post-loop n (which is 0) is a classic bug.

**Why negatives are never palindromes.** -121 written out is `-121`; reversed it would read `121-`, which isn't a valid number — so by convention negatives return false. Reject them up front.

**The half-reversal optimisation.** You can stop after reversing only half the digits and compare halves, which avoids any overflow concern. For a fresher answer, full reverse-and-compare is perfectly acceptable — but mentioning the half-reverse shows depth.
hints: What does 'reads the same backwards' mean in terms of reversing the digits?
Reverse the number, then compare to the original — but save the original first.
Handle negatives up front: by convention they're not palindromes.
approaches.insight: A space-savvy variant reverses only half the digits, but reverse-and-compare is perfectly acceptable for a fresher answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: one reversal pass over the digits plus an equality check — proportional to the digit count.

dryRun.intro: Reverse, then compare to the saved original.

edgeCases.behavior: Rejected up front — negatives aren't palindromes → false.

pitfalls: Comparing `rev` against the mutated n (now 0) instead of the saved original.

commonMistakes: Comparing against `n` after the loop has already reduced it to 0 (save the original first).
